text.p: Anglo-U.S. conglomerate Hanson Plc sent out full details of its planned demerger on Wednesday, showing that its plans to spin off two companies this year and one more in early 1997 remain on track.
As expected, the demergers of Imperial Tobacco Group Plc and Millennium Chemicals Inc are due to be effective from October 1.
"Excellent management is in place and I look forward with great confidence to their future performance," Lord Hanson said of the first two new offspring in a letter to shareholders.

Imperial Tobacco said it looking to build on a history of cost-cutting under the Hanson umbrella, with its focus now on exports. "Ours is an export-led strategy," Imperial chief executive Gareth Davis told Reuters.

Davis said Imperial's float with approximately 1.1 billion pounds of debt was within market expectations and said the valuation of Imperial, which will be effective from October 1, was "something the market will decide at the end of the day".
He stressed the company's cash-generative nature, saying that in its 1994/95 year it converted 99 percent of its operating profit into cash, generating some 345 million pounds ($537.3 million).

Davis said in the period of ownership by Hanson, the company had improved its cigarette-manufacturing productivity by 195 percent and said its return on sales figure of 46 percent was the highest of any of its competitors.
Imperial, whose brands include John Player Special, Superkings and Embassy, has increased its share of the British cigarette market to 38 percent from below 33 percent in 1990.
This, however, is in the context of a market which has declined by two percent per year, leading the company to focus more on overseas.
Davis said the export strategy was firstly to achieve a higher penetration of continental European markets and secondly to expand in the massive Asia-Pacific market.
"It's early days yet but Greater China offers significant opportunities for us," he said.
Davis said Imperial was confident of its defences against potential health-related litigation from smokers.
"We are very confident that we have very strong defences and will defend any case with the utmost vigour," he said.
Unlike its sector rival B.A.T Industries, Imperial, is not a large player in the U.S. market, but Davis said he followed reports of litigation there.

Davis echoed B.A.T in saying that a verdict last week in Indiana in favour of tobacco companies showed that an earlier case in Florida where a jury ruled in favour of the plaintiff was "something of an aberration", and he noted that the Florida verdict was subject to appeal.
"There have been some 700 cases since the mid-50s and not one cent paid in damages," Davis said.

Shareholders will be asked to approve the two demergers at an extraordinary general meeting on September 25. Dealings in Imperial are expected to start on October 1, while Millennium is expected to start trading on the NYSE on October 2.
The Energy Group, the third part of the Hanson group to be separated out, will remain in Hanson until early 1997.

Millennium and Imperial are predominantly U.S.- and British-based companies respectively, but Energy will mix one large U.S.-based business, Peabody Coal, and a major British electricity generator and distirbutor, Eastern Group.

Once Energy has left the fold, the remainder of Hanson Plc will be a building materials and services group with interests ranging from bricks in Europe to aggregates, asphalt and crane hire in many countries, including the United States. ($1=.6421 Pound)
